body: The last morning of summer, and Marisol is showing off. At twelve past seven the light comes into 412 low and level off the Lagoon, which lies out there flat as a plate, not a ripple on it, and the window is cracked its two inches on the Grove, so the room smells of eucalyptus with nothing to damp it down: menthol, dust, a little cat. No fog all week, says the forecast on Theo’s phone.

Two cards are lying on the carpet inside the door where somebody slid them under it in the night. Black borders. Heavy stock. The borders were ruled by hand and cut with scissors by someone who believes in doing a thing properly and doesn’t own a paper cutter, and not one corner of either card is square. Jack picks up the one with his name on it.

body.title: Under the door, 412
body.text:
IN MEMORIAM
DJARUM BLACK
Kudus, Central Java — Marisol, California, September 22, 2009
*It crackled.*

A wake will be held on the Delgado roof from sundown until the last one is gone.
The eulogy will be delivered at 1:30 a.m., to accommodate the dish pit.

Bring pie, Costigan. The good pie.
Bring the other Catholic.

—M.L.

body: It’s the first he’s heard of any wake. It is, as far as he can tell, the first thing Margot Lindqvist has ever invited him to that wasn’t an argument. The other card is addressed in the same square capitals.

body.title: Under the door, 412 (the other one)
body.text:
Mr. Vance, mourner.
Black tie optional.
Do not film.
—M.L.

body: From under the Frette a hand comes out, palm up. Jack puts the card in it. The hand withdraws, and then Theo’s voice, thick with whatever sleep he got: “I’m going to film.”
The Dell is open on Jack’s desk where he left it, still logged in, and overnight his wall has grown a post.

body: Theo already knows. The iPhone is lit under the sheet; he reads everything about Jack before Jack does, on principle. “Friday,” he says, “you have a date with the cattle baroness.” “She can butcher a deer.” The sheet comes down. Theo turns his head on the pillow, all the way, slowly, to look at him. “Say that again. Slower. I want to remember where I was.” “She told me at the cleanup. She’s pulled a calf.” Theo lies back with the iPhone on his chest, enchanted, already casting it. Then, lightly, still scrolling: “You told me you weren’t doing anything. I believed you.” A sigh, with some craft in it. “I’m a very trusting person.”

The Benedict holy card comes out of Hale’s Williams, which goes onto the desk with its one pencilled *No.* and the rest of its margins still owed, and into the Augustine — the Penguin *Confessions*, Pine-Coffin’s translation, CARDINAL MOONEY H.S. LIBRARY — DISCARD in purple down the page edges, a dime off the cart junior spring — at Book Four, which is Wednesday, and the Augustine goes into his back pocket.

response: Theo doesn’t open his eyes. “Costigan. There are two of you in this building.” He pulls the Frette up to his chin. “She’s being *inclusive*.”
Jack takes the card with him to his nine o’clock in his shirt pocket, and the black border shows above the hem the whole way across the Commons.

choices.text: “She scheduled the eulogy around my shift.”
response: Theo sits up for this. “That is the most romantic thing Margot Lindqvist has ever done,” he says, “and she’ll deny it at gunpoint.” He seems moved. He lies back down to recover from it.
Jack goes to his nine o’clock with the card in his shirt pocket, black border showing: half-mourning, for something he never smoked.

choices.text: Put the card in the Augustine and go to class.
response: The card goes in at Book Four, next to the Pope. Theo, to the ceiling, as Jack shoulders his backpack: “Black tie optional.” A wounded pause. “She’s never met me.”
Jack is out the door to his nine o’clock before Theo can decide which tie.

body: Twelve-ten on a Tuesday at St. Brendan’s is twenty people and a great deal of boat. The ceiling goes up over them in its long overturned hull, and the noon light comes down through the blue glass and lies across the pews in panels the color of a swimming pool after dark. Green on the altar, green on the priest: Ordinary Time, the long green middle of the year. Mrs. Fitch in her pew by the shrine with her purse squared on her knees. The old man with the cane, who takes the aisle seat and always will. Two rows up, Becca Lindell, braid down her back to the belt, a rosary wound twice around her wrist; a 12:10 regular, it turns out, in between labs. And Kevin in his navy quarter-zip, who has saved Jack a seat with a Bible open on it to the day’s Gospel.

Lena comes in during the opening prayer. Bare-headed, no lace today, the oatmeal cardigan over a green dress, and she slides into the pew on Jack’s other side without a word or a look, genuflecting so fast it’s mostly knee, and folds her hands in her lap like she has been there since the bell.

Osei is saying the whole Mass himself, as he said he would. He reads the Gospel too. Luke, eight: Jesus in a house so full that his own family can’t get through the door, and somebody has to pass the message over the heads of the crowd. *Your mother and your brothers are standing outside, and they wish to see you.* “My mother and my brothers,” Osei reads, “are those who hear the word of God and act on it.”
Jack hears *brothers*.

Osei doesn’t go to the ambo to preach. He stands where he read, takes the reading glasses off their cord, and says two sentences to the twenty of them. “They could not get in for the crowd. He does not send them away — he makes the room bigger.” Then he goes to his chair and sits, and the church is quiet enough to hear the old man’s cane slide along the pew.

At the prayers of the faithful he reads the intentions off an index card in his own hand: the sick, the dead, the President. And last, without lifting his eyes from the card: “For the intention of Carmela Rinaldi, in thanksgiving.” He gives it nothing else. No grandmother, no grandson, no reason. Lena was right there a week ago Sunday when Mrs. Fitch read the whole slip out loud, *good confession* and all. She keeps her eyes on the altar. The corner of her mouth tucks in, very slightly, until the Our Father.

After the blessing Kevin squeezes Jack’s shoulder, mouths *orgo* with tragic eyebrows, and is gone up the aisle at a jog. Osei catches Jack in the vestibule, still in the green, and hands him an envelope.

body.title: A Mass card, St. Brendan the Navigator
body.text:
The Holy Sacrifice of the Mass
will be offered for
Carmela Rinaldi
in thanksgiving

Tuesday, September 22, 2009 · 12:10 p.m.
Rev. Gabriel K. Osei, celebrant

body: “A grandmother likes paper,” Osei says. “Mail it today. At her age a letter is a house call.” “Thank you, Father.” “*Me da wo ase* is the correct reply,” Osei says, delighted with him, “but you will get there,” and limps off toward the sacristy.

Lena is at the Marian shrine with a dollar in the box and a taper, lighting one candle low on the rack. When she comes back up the side aisle she says, “For Carmela,” as if he’d asked. Then, lower, walking out: “Did you tell him I said he’s welcome?” “Mailed it yesterday.” She nods once. “Did she ask you twice again?” “Haven’t called.” “Call.”

Becca is waiting outside the door in the full sun, Wranglers and a Carhartt vest and a spiral planner under her arm, and she doesn’t bother with hello. “Friday. Six. I’ll drive. I have a truck.” She holds up a key ring on a steel carabiner. “My brother Eli’s. A Ranger.” She beams past him. “Hi, Lena!” And she’s off across the courtyard at a ranch walk, late for a lab, the braid swinging.

Lena watches her all the way to Ocean Road. “She has a truck.” “Her brother’s. A Ranger.” “Of course she has a truck.” She says it with real admiration. Then she turns and looks at him, kind and exact, and it’s the lifeguard tower again, Sunday, the same words in the same order: “Find out what you’re doing, Costigan.”

Before he can do anything with that she has a black-bordered card out of her cardigan pocket, its corners as crooked as his. “Mine says bring the other Catholic.” “That’s me.” “Yours says it too?” “Bring the other Catholic.” She looks at the card, at the olive tree, at him. “Then we’re each other’s plus-one.”

journal.title: Fr. Gabriel Osei
journal.text: Newman chaplain. Kumasi, Ghana. Used to be a doctor. Limps and doesn’t mention it. Plays chess like he’s got all night and highlife like the neighbors owe him money. Told me a proverb about funerals. I laughed. That was apparently the point. Said Nonna’s Mass himself at the 12:10, like he promised. Gave me a card for her: ‘A grandmother likes paper.’

response: “Somebody has to hold the hymnal,” Lena says. It starts out as a joke. Somewhere around *hymnal* it stops being one, and she leaves it like that and puts the card back in her pocket.
At one o’clock he mails Nonna’s card at the UCen post-office counter, first class, forty-four cents, and watches the clerk drop it in the tub for Ohio.
“She is,” Lena says. “I said so first.” Pleasant. Exact. Done. The card goes back in the cardigan pocket, and she goes down the steps toward the Grove with her hands in after it.
At one o’clock he mails Nonna’s card at the UCen post-office counter, forty-four cents, first class to Glenwood Avenue.

choices.text: “I’m going to explain football to her.”
response: “Let her explain it to you,” Lena says, already walking. “She’ll be better at it.” Over her shoulder, the card held up between two knuckles like a ticket: “Sundown, Catholic.”
At one o’clock he mails Nonna’s card at the UCen post-office counter, and the clerk asks if it’s a birthday, and he says, more or less.

The room has the five o’clock smell of a dorm in September, warm carpet and somebody’s microwave popcorn coming down the hall. Jack has an hour and change before the Anchor, and he spends it the way the whole fourth floor spends that hour, at the secondhand Dell with its fan going like a hair dryer, refreshing Facebook.
The news feed has his sister in it.

body: Half-price chowder Tuesday is down to its last pot and its last four customers, and for the first time since seven the dish pit has caught up with itself. The Hobart lets out its steam on the cycle and the steam goes up into the light over the pass and hangs there. Somebody has put a quarter in the jukebox for Patsy Cline, “Walkin’ After Midnight,” which at twenty to twelve is a little on the nose, and Gloria gives the jukebox a look on her way by with the pot. Over the register the chalkboard says PIE OF THE DAY: PECAN in her capitals, and on the board beside it, the one she put up for him his first week, JACK’S RATINGS: MARIONBERRY 4/10 · OLALLIEBERRY 9/10.

On the far stool by the kitchen, Ray Ochoa is eating the meatloaf. Tuesdays, meatloaf, black coffee: he said so on Ocean Road with his badge wallet open, and here he is in the navy windbreaker, a man as good as his word. When the plate came up in the window he lifted his chin a quarter inch at Rudy, and Rudy, behind the heat lamps, lifted his back, and that was the whole conversation; from the ease of it, it’s been going on for years. Ray eats like there’s a clock somewhere only he can see. At 11:52 he leaves a ten under the saucer and zips the windbreaker, and passing the end of the pass, without turning his head: “Light working, Mr. Costigan?” “Yes, sir.” “Good.” The bell over the door. The gray Crown Vic backs out under the wharf lamp and is gone up Mission.

At midnight Jack asks Gloria if she’ll sell him a whole pie. “For what?” “A funeral.” Gloria sets the pot on the warmer. “Whose?” “A cigarette’s.” At the flattop Rudy, back to both of them, who has been listening to every word the way he listens to Vin Scully, crosses himself with the spatula hand and goes on scraping.

Gloria wants all of it: whose cigarette, who’s burying it, and who the pie is *for*. Jack does his best. All black, he says. From Portland. No body temperature anybody has ever measured. Keeps a whiteboard in the fourth-floor lounge with his name on it and a running score. Says he upholds the patriarchy. “Do you?” “I wash dishes, Gloria.” She closes her eyes, the pencil in the gray bun, and rates her sight unseen. “Rhubarb. Tart, and nobody can decide if it’s a fruit.” “It’s a vegetable.” “It’s a vegetable, hon. That’s the point.” She has rhubarb in the freezer since June and one pie baked off it sitting in the case, untouched. “Nobody’s complained,” Gloria says. “Nobody orders it.”
“Who else is going?” “The other Catholic.” Gloria looks at him over the pot, the look she gave the jukebox. She doesn’t ask which.

A whole pie is sixteen dollars. She writes eight on the ticket and underlines it twice. “Bereavement discount.” He pays it out of tonight’s tips, which come to eleven dollars and a Canadian quarter, and she takes the eight and slides the quarter back across the Formica, because it’s Canadian. Then she puts her hand on top of the pie case. “So. Which.”

journal.title: The Anchor
journal.text: Marionberry: 4/10. Olallieberry: 9/10 — Dad would eat two pieces and complain about the second. Gloria rated Lena: pecan. She rated Margot without meeting her: rhubarb — tart, and nobody can decide if it’s a fruit. A whole pie for a funeral is half price. Bereavement discount. I work here Tue/Thu/Sat, seven to one.

choices.key: You brought Margot’s wake the good pie by your own board: olallieberry, a nine.
response: Gloria nods as if he’s passed something, lifts it out of the case, and boxes it in white cardboard with the string done up in a bakery knot. “Your board,” she says, “your funeral.”
At 1:15 he’s out the back door with the box in La Flaca’s basket and Ray’s light blinking on the handlebars, three miles of Ocean Road and a roof to make by half past.

choices.key: You let Gloria pick the funeral pie. She picked pecan.
response: Gloria doesn’t take long. She opens the case and lifts out the pie of the day. “Pecan,” she says. “Trust me.” She boxes it and ties the string and slides it across, and that’s the end of the discussion as far as Gloria is concerned.
At 1:15 he’s out the back door with the box in La Flaca’s basket and Ray’s light blinking on the handlebars, three miles of Ocean Road and a roof to make by half past.

choices.key: You brought Margot a rhubarb pie: tart, and nobody can decide if it’s a fruit.
response: Gloria laughs out loud, which brings Rudy’s head around from the flattop. “Now you’re rating people,” she says, boxing it. “I’ll make a waitress of you yet.”
At 1:15 he’s out the back door with the box in La Flaca’s basket and Ray’s light blinking on the handlebars, three miles of Ocean Road and a roof to make by half past.

body: Hollis 302 empties the way a seminar empties after a fight: fast, and pretending it isn’t. Caleb rounds up his Post-its. Yusuf caps his pen and leaves his load diagrams on the table for somebody else to worry about. The Palo Alto girl is in the hall on her phone before the door has closed. The afternoon lies along the table, the sea in the window gone white with glare, and Lena’s chair stands pushed back at an angle, the way she left it, with her paper gone and his gone with it.
Hale stays perched on the table’s end with one long leg swinging. The linen jacket has its wine on the cuff. “How are my margins?” “One.” “One is a beginning.”

body.text: He reaches inside the jacket and comes out with a book the size of a deck of cards. *A Shropshire Lad*, a pocket edition, the paper browned and freckled through — foxed — the cloth worn to the board at the corners, and on the back of the title page, in small capitals, a notice that the book has been produced in complete conformity with the authorized economy standards. Wartime. It was made to go in a pocket and through a war. Hale sets it on the table and moves it across the wood toward Jack with one finger. “For the brother,” he says. “No margins. They’d only erase them.”
body.else: Then he lifts the finger again, toward the door, and lets him go.

body.text: Jack picks it up and it falls open by itself, where it’s been opened before. LIV. *With rue my heart is laden / For golden friends I had.* He knows the rest. Mrs. Pagliarulo made the whole junior class learn it, and two weeks ago, at half past twelve at night in the Anchor’s back booth, he finished it for a drunk man who was saying it to the window. He holds the book open at the page, and in the window the sea goes on being white.

choices.key: Hale gave you a pocket Housman for your brother. You thanked him.

journal.title: Prof. Adrian Hale
journal.text: Wrote *The Consolations of Disbelief*. Wrote me a postcard. Walked into Hollis 302 at 1:07 with wine on his cuff and asked us to prove we have souls. Saw my face at the Anchor before he could put it to the nine pages. Called me a spaniel. Some nights he drinks alone in the Anchor’s back booth after midnight and says Housman to the window. Tips like he’s apologizing. Wrote his doctorate on moral luck. Asked me if the lucky one sleeps. Lent me his own copy of Williams’s *Moral Luck*; wants it back with my margins in it. I owe him more than one. Gave me a pocket Housman for Danny, foxed, wartime. No margins. They’d only erase them.

response: Hale waves it off like smoke, a quick flap of the hand by his ear, and gets down off the table to look for his reading glasses, which are on his head.

Jack is asleep in 412 by ten past three, on top of the blanket in yesterday’s jeans with the Housman under his hand. He sleeps through the afternoon and the light going and wakes at nine in the dark. The RAZR has been holding something since 4:17.

response.text: Brother. Waited 40 min at the Jamba Juice. Praying for you anyway. Praying HARDER.

response: He turns on the desk lamp, takes the cap off a red pen, and bleeds on her paper until two.

s11.slug: SATURDAY · 12:40 PM · DELGADO HALL, EAST STAIRWELL, 4TH-FLOOR LANDING
body: At twenty to one on a Saturday the east stairwell is the warmest room in Delgado. The sun has been on the landing window since eleven and the concrete has drunk it, and the window is open its six inches on a Lagoon so blue it looks retouched. Jack sits on the top step with his back to the wall. The RAZR is wedged into the top corner of the frame, where the one good bar lives. Ohio State beat Illinois this morning while he watched the second half on Theo’s MacBook with Theo asleep beside it: a shutout, and Theo woke up long enough to ask who Pryor was.

Twenty to four on Glenwood Avenue. His mother picks up with the TV going behind her and starts in the middle. Pittsburgh has been on the news all week, she tells him, the G-20, every president in the world, protesters with bandanas over their faces and the bridges shut down, sixty-some miles away and you’d think it was the moon. Then, quick, tucked in between the bridges and the next thing: his father has a meeting at the union hall Tuesday. Then the next thing. “Nonna’s card came yesterday. From your priest. She put it on the refrigerator next to Rosie’s crab, Jackie. She made Mrs. Iannucci come in and look at it.”
A click, the extension in the front room, and the post-game show comes in behind it. “Thirty-nothing,” his father says. “Shutout.” “I saw.” “Good.” Click.
Then his mother, in a different voice, the one she uses at the school office for parents who are behind on tuition: “Who’s Idaho?”

choices.text: “Her name’s Becca. Seven brothers and sisters. A ranch.”
response: “*Seven!*” His mother says it the way other people say *jackpot*. “Catholic?” “Very.” A kitchen chair scrapes. Somewhere behind her, from the direction of the stairs, Gina, at full volume: “*SHE DRIVES.*”
“A girl from church,” his mother repeats, in a tone that forgets nothing. “Gina says she drives.”
“Idaho is *somebody*,” his mother says. “Gina showed me her picture on the computer. She looks like a nice girl.” Then a pause with *you never tell me anything* in it.

s11b.slug: SATURDAY · 12:51 PM · DELGADO HALL, EAST STAIRWELL, 4TH-FLOOR LANDING
body: Gina gets shooed. A door shuts somewhere on Glenwood Avenue. The dishwasher starts its rinse, and Rosie is singing to herself in another room, and his mother leaves the line quiet for a second with all of that in it.
“And the veil girl?”

choices.key: Your mother asked about the veil girl. You told her she has a boyfriend.
response: A pause on Glenwood Avenue. The dishwasher. The TV. Rosie, somewhere, still singing.
“Oh, honey.”
When she talks again it’s to say, “Eat something,” which is how she says goodbye, and he says he will, and at seven he’s in the dish pit with his sleeves past his elbows.

“Okay,” his mother says, the way she says okay when it means she’ll be back for the rest of it. Then: “Eat something.” He says he will, and at seven he’s in the dish pit with his sleeves past his elbows.

His mother laughs, the Rinaldi laugh with the snort on the end that she has been trying to get rid of since the eighth grade. Then it goes. “Okay,” she says. Then: “Eat something.” He says he will, and at seven he’s in the dish pit with his sleeves past his elbows.
